commitments.text: Due to the history of the area, the baseline geochemical analyses of water quality at the site should include mercury, and the proponent should clearly document baseline concentrations of all heavy metals and other potential environmental contaminants. Baseline surveys and later monitoring should be performed both upstream and downstream of the proposed facility in order to isolate any effects linked to the facility.

The baseline geochemical study should recognize that seasonal variations in water quality are quite likely. Sampling, with a complete suite of analyses, should be performed at different times of the year corresponding to different hydrological conditions.

The proponent should document baseline water quality in domestic wells that may be affected by the development, since aquifers receiving greater recharge from the river, particularly in summer months, may impact water quality in wells drawing from these aquifers.

The report's geological characterization relies on unreliable/limited sources; NRCan notes extensive relevant Geological Survey of Canada literature (~100 publications for the Kettle River area) and research on the Kettle River Fault, and recommends the geological interpretation supporting the Acid Rock Drainage and Nitrate Released by Blasting assessment be based on adequate, reliable geological information.

The ARD report concludes the rock surfaces exposed by blasting will not be acid generating, but notes this is preliminary being based on only four samples and that more intensive sampling and testing will be required at a later stage to confirm. NRCan concurs the investigation is preliminary and suggests further study of the geology, preferably by an experienced geotechnical engineer.

The bedrock and surficial geology of the site and surrounds are not mapped or described in detail. A detailed description of the foundation conditions at the weir location should be provided to characterise rock mass conditions vis-a-vis leakage, and the extent of potentially hazardous glaciolacustrine sediments should be addressed.

The presence of landslides in surficial deposits along the pondage is acknowledged, but the possibility of rapid slumps and slides generating waves in a narrow, confined pondage created by a weir (a dam with no freeboard) is not considered; this is an important consideration in view of tourist use downstream of the weir.

No consideration is given to the valley side environment directly adjacent to the project, including whether there are mountain slope instability features that suggest the possibility of large-scale rock slope failure that could impact the project site. NRCan concludes that geological and geotechnical issues of the Project are not adequately addressed in the Application or its Appendices.
